utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. You're not under arrest. You can leave whenever you want. Coffee?
I'm good. What's this about?
The fire at Kessler's Garage last Tuesday night. You worked there, right?
Two years. I quit in June. Look, I already told the other officer — I wasn't anywhere near that place that night.
And before you ask, yeah, I know how it looks. But that red plastic fuel can they found? That's not mine. I've never owned one of those.
Nobody said anything about a fuel can until just now.
It was on the news. Everyone knows.
Fair enough. Let's talk about how you got in.
I didn't get in anywhere. But I'll tell you what — that back service door behind the shop, the one by the dumpster? It never latched right. Anyone could've walked through it.
So you knew the rear door was faulty.
Everyone who worked there knew. It's not a secret.
Okay. Tell me about Tuesday evening. Start at dinner.
Ate at home. Watched a bit of the game. Then I went out for a drive to clear my head.
It was chilly, so I grabbed my gray hoodie — the pullover one with the hood — and just drove around.
The gray hooded sweatshirt. Do you still have it?
Somewhere in my closet, yeah.
We'll need to take a look at it. Now — the fire was reported at eleven-forty p.m. Where were you at 11:40?
I was home. In bed, probably.
Can anyone confirm that?
I live alone.
So nobody can place you at home at twenty to midnight.
I told you — I was in bed around 11:40. That's what I said.
Let's go back to the drive. What were you driving?
My blue hatchback. The little one. It's nothing fancy.
The blue hatchback — is that the only car you have access to?
It's the only one I've got, yeah.
Did anyone see that car near the garage that night?
How would I know? I wasn't there.
Okay. Let's talk about your arm.
The paramedics mentioned a burn on the right forearm. How'd that happen?
I don't have a burn. I don't know what you're talking about.
Roll up your sleeve and we'll clear it up right now.
I'm not doing that. And I never said anything about a burn.
That's fine. It's noted. Let's take a break — you want some water?
Sure. Actually — one thing. I take the bus a lot. The depot on Mill Street, that's my stop. If you're checking cameras, check there.
The bus depot on Mill Street. Why bring that up?
Because I was on a bus that night. That's my alibi. The depot cameras will show me.
We'll pull those. What time was that bus?
Late. After eleven. I don't remember exactly.
Funny. You remember the fuel can, the back door, your hoodie, your car, the depot — but not the time.
I remember what I remember.
One last thing. Did you ever go back to that garage after you quit?
No. Not once.
Alright. We're done for now. Don't leave town.

utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. You understand you're not under arrest, and you can leave whenever you want. We're just trying to sort out what happened at the Ridgeway warehouse last Tuesday.
Yeah, I get it. I don't know what I can tell you, though. I wasn't there.
That's fine. Let's start simple. Do you have any connection to the loading dock keycard system at Ridgeway?
The keycard thing? No. I never had one of those.
Okay. Where were you that night, roughly between eleven and midnight?
Home. Watching something. I don't really remember.
Look, I'll be straight with you — I did borrow a green Transit van from my cousin that week. But that's not a crime.
A green Transit. Okay. Who's your cousin?
Marek. He lives over on Delaney. He lets people borrow it sometimes.
And did that van end up anywhere near Ridgeway that night?
I don't think so. I was just running errands.
Let's talk about the alarm system. Records show it was silenced at about 11:40 p.m. Does that time mean anything to you?
Eleven forty? No, I was already home by then.
The panel was bypassed, not smashed. Someone knew the code or had the right access. That sound like anyone you know?
I wouldn't know anything about that.
Fair enough. Now — when you were out that evening, what were you wearing?
Just normal stuff. Jeans, a jacket.
We've got camera footage from a nearby lot. The person in it is wearing a blue hooded sweatshirt. Do you own something like that?
A blue hoodie? I mean, yeah, I've got a hoodie. Half the city does.
Sure. But this one's fairly distinctive — royal blue, logo on the chest. We'd like to see yours.
I can probably find it. It's just a sweatshirt.
Let's go back to the warehouse. What do you think was taken?
No idea. I don't work there.
The inventory sheet shows a pallet of cordless power tools came up missing. Drills, saws, that kind of thing. Any thoughts on where those might have gone?
Power tools? I wouldn't know where to sell something like that.
Nobody said anything about selling. I just asked where they might have gone.
Right. I'm just saying I don't know.
Okay. Let's take a break. Can I get you a water?
Yeah, sure. Thanks.
While we're waiting — anything else you want to tell me about that night?
Not really. I mean, the fence out back was already cut when I drove past, if that's what you're getting at.
You drove past? Where exactly did you see a cut fence?
Behind the lot on Ridgeway. The chain-link was sliced open. I figured it was kids.
Interesting. We hadn't mentioned the fence yet.
I'm just telling you what I saw.
Let's go back over the keycard again. You're sure you never had access to the loading dock?
Yeah. Never.
And the alarm going quiet at 11:40 — that fits with someone who knew the building.
Yeah, I guess it would.
The blue hoodie — we're going to need it. And the van.
Yeah, fine. The hoodie, the van, whatever.
And those cordless tools — the drills and saws from that pallet — if they turn up at a pawn shop, we'll know.
The drills and saws. Right. I already told you I don't know anything about a pallet of tools.
Okay. I think we've got enough for now. We'll be in touch.
Can I go?
You can go. But don't leave town.

I couldn't tell you. I wasn't checking my phone.

I already said no. I can't help you with that one.
